lignes.texte: The grid went dark. The internet died. Then the city starved.
There were no warnings. No explanations. Just millions
of people plunged into absolute chaos… and the clock is ticking.
The old world isn’t coming back. The only question is… will you be alive to see what comes next.
Day 1
Everyday, Nate Kessler watches 5,400 miles (8,690 km) of water snaking through the pipes
of Cleveland. For 23 years, he’s sat in front of a wall of flashing screens… and watched.
It is one of the most boring jobs in America. And Nate is very good at it.
Until 4:16.
The power meter on his console drops from 60 hertz to 59.3 hertz. It’s not much,
but it’s below the critical threshold for the grid to function.
Every light in the building snaps off.
11 seconds later the emergency generator coughs to life. The screens boot back up,
but the data fields are empty. Thousands of sensors across the city flatline. The
landlines are just dead air. Someone jokes about a squirrel hitting a transformer.
Nate doesn’t laugh. He just writes a standard entry in the shift log:
1617hours Commercial power lost. Cause unknown.
He has no idea he just logged the end of the modern world.
It is 94 degrees F (34.4 C). Every traffic light on the west side is dark. Cleveland drivers can’t
handle 200 of them in a row. Within half an hour, road rage has exploded on the city’s streets.
Nate’s 20 minute drive home takes an agonizing 90 minutes. At one intersection, 2 drivers are out of
their cars, screaming at each other. One grabs a tire iron and smashes out the other’s headlights.
Nobody steps in.
The AM radio says the outage covers 4 states and part of Canada. Nate isn’t
worried. He lived through the August 2003 blackout. It took 2 days for
the system to come back online. He expects this outage to be the same.
He’s wrong.
At his 14 story apartment building, the elevators are dead. Walt Pruitt, president of the condo
board, is already taping a laminated sign to the lobby door thanking residents for their patience.
Up on the 11th floor, Nate’s kitchen faucet splutters and belches out air.
The building’s booster pump has lost pressure. But the lobby sink still
works. Nate grabs 2 5-gallon (19 liter) buckets, walks down 11 flights and hauls
them back up. He repeats the climb 4 times until the bathtub is full.
His wife Dana, an ICU nurse, watches him dump the last bucket. She asks if
he’s starting a trout farm. His daughter Priya panics because her phone is at 14%.
Nate doesn’t care about the phone. He’s focused on the fridge. Specifically,
a yellow sticky note stuck under a magnet that reads “Insulin,
top shelf.” Priya’s insulin. Without power, the fridge, and that medication, are on a countdown.
By 9 p.m., the building’s residents move to the roof. The freezers are all thawing,
so the steaks come out, along with three charcoal grills. For the first time in memory, Cleveland
can see the Milky Way. Neighbors who haven’t spoken for years share drinks. It feels quaint.
It feels like a community.
It won’t feel like that much longer.
At 2:04 in the morning, Nate’s work radio crackles to life. The city’s water pumps have 48 hours of
backup diesel left. The electric utility isn’t answering… because it doesn’t exist anymore.
Nate reaches for his phone. No Service.
Across the city, hundreds of cell towers have fallen offline. Their backup batteries,
which typically last 4 to 8 hours, have bled dry. The digital world is officially gone.
Nate rolls out of bed and opens his log book. Day 1, 0204 hours:
Pump stations report 48 hours of diesel. No response from the grid.
Then he picks up the empty buckets and walks into the darkness.
Day 2
At 5:30 a.m., Dana takes Priya’s bicycle and rides to the hospital.
Nobody can call her in, but as an ICU nurse, she knows they’re short staffed
and completely blind. Before she goes, she leaves a note on the kitchen counter.
Keep the freezer closed. Check Priya’s sugar
before lunch. Do not let your father lecture anyone about water pressure.
By noon, the kitchen thermometer reads 91 degrees F (33 C). Nate holds the instruction
insert from Priya's insulin box and reads it. It’s probably the first time in 8 years,
at least since she was diagnosed. Insulin can go 28 days without refrigeration,
but only between 59 and 86 degrees F (15-30 C). Above that, it starts to lose strength.
The fridge has been dead for hours, and the apartment passed 86 degrees F (30 C) before
breakfast. Nate seals 4 vials in a Mason jar, treks down the stairs, and sets it on the lowest
shelf of his storage cage in the basement. It’s cooler down here and hopefully buys him some time.
The basement is silent as Nate steps in. Then he hears the shrill clang of metal on metal.
He turns a corner and sees Dale Brandt, a resident from the 6th floor standing
in the aisle with a crowbar in his hand. A broken padlock lies on the concrete floor.
Dale steps inside a neighbor’s storage cage and pulls out camping
gear and a stove. He stuffs them into a backpack and spins around,
spotting Nate. The two men stare at each other, the crowbar hanging limply in Dale’s hand.
Dale smirks and walks past Nate, the stolen camping gear slung over his
shoulder. Nate’s heart hammers in his chest as he runs to his cage.
The padlock is still intact. He unlocks it and places the Mason jar on the lowest shelf,
behind a stack of old tires and closes the mesh door. He wonders how long the padlock will last.
Priya follows him down a few minutes later. She asks if everything will be ok.Nate looks his
daughter in her eyes and tells her it’s fine. They both know he’s lying, but no one says anything.
By afternoon, a crowd empties a few stores on Brookpark Road. Men scramble
for crates of bottled water, batteries and preserved food, hauling down the sidewalk.
Cash is the other surprise. The ATMs are all dead. The card readers are dead. The corner
store takes bills only, with no change since the owner can’t open the register. Priya digs $43
of birthday money from a sock drawer, instantly becoming the wealthiest member of the household.
Nate writes the evening entry by flashlight. Day 2, 1900 hours:
Zone 2 pressure is holding on generator power. Every elevated tank on the west side is falling.
Day 3
Only 3 of Nate’s 9 man crew show up for work. The others can’t get gas. When the power went out,
the station pumps went with it. It had been a similar story after Hurricane Sandy,
where about 60% of the stations in New Jersey closed for the same reason.
Worse, the water department’s emergency diesel supply is stranded. The terminal can’t load a
truck without electricity, and neither can the pipeline that fills it. The pumps that
push fuel through refined product pipelines run on the exact same grid that is currently dead.
Every terminal from Ohio to the Atlantic is down.
Hospitals claim first priority. The water department sits lower on the list.
At 11 a.m, a mob arrives at the water department’s gates. They carry buckets, water coolers and jugs.
They start hammering on the security doors, screaming for the water lines to be switched
back on. Nate’s supervisor orders the facility to be locked down. Nate watches through a window
which seconds later, explodes in a spider’s web of cracks. Someone just launched a brick at it.
The city is getting thirsty.
At 2:10 in the afternoon, the tank on the hill above Zone 2 reads empty.
Cleveland is officially dry.
That night, the inevitable happens.
A pharmacy looting turns into a violent brawl between rival blocks. Someone throws a petrol
bomb through the store window. It doesn’t take long for the fire to
get out of control. The flames jump from one building to the next, including a 90 year old
wood framed double. By the time the first engine arrives, the fire is in the attic,
the elderly occupants are dead, and the blaze is moving onto the house next door.
Nate is walking home in his water department jacket when the
firefighters wrench open the hydrant on the corner. It coughs, hisses,
and dribbles into the gutter. The captain spots Nate’s jacket and shoves him toward the hydrant.
Nate tries to explain. Fire hydrants run on the same pressure as the kitchen
faucet. The tanks are completely empty. The captain stares at him for a moment,
before realizing the scale of the situation. He pushes Nate away and runs back to his crew.
The engine's tank lasts about 4 minutes. After that,
the crew starts pulling people from the houses on either side.
There’s nothing else they can do.
The house turns into glowing embers. Smoke and ash float into the night sky.
All Nate can do is open his notebook and scribble in a note. Day 3, 2140 hours:
Hydrant 4471 no flow. 6 structures were lost.
Day 4
Dana finishes 61 gruelling hours at the hospital.
Someone stole the bike out of the staff courtyard, so she has to walk back. On the way,
she passes a nursing home on Lorain Avenue with its front doors propped
open and nobody at the desk. She steps inside, and finds the staff abandoning
the residents to check on their own families. The night staff never came in to relieve them.
The second floor suffocates under a wave of urine and heat.
Dana’s mind flashes to the aftermath of Hurricane Irma, when a nursing home in Florida had lost its
air conditioning. Indoor temperatures reached 99 degrees F (37.2 C). 12 residents baked to death.
Dana spends the next 2 hours prying open windows and carrying cups of water from a
rain barrel. She’s refilling a cup when she hears a commotion in the kitchen.
Peering through a broken window, she spots a group of young men tearing the room apart,
looking for food. She hides behind a linen cart until they leave.
By the time she stumbles into her apartment, her scrubs are stained with sweat. She slumps
on the kitchen floor. She doesn’t even speak. Eventually, she looks at Priya’s glucose monitor.
212. And rising.
Nate needs to get the insulin. He forces his aching feet back
into his work boots and forces himself back down the pitch black stairwell.
Day 5
The freezers in the building have been dead for 96 hours.
Walt Pruitt, the building president, calls a mandatory barbeque. Residents
lug everything they have down to the parking garage. Someone tries to light the charcoal
grills until Walt points out carbon monoxide poisoning will kill them before starvation.
Everyone moves out to the driveway.
There are lobster tails, venison from a hunter on seven, pierogies, and the frozen top tier
of a wedding cake that a couple on floor 12 have been saving for their first anniversary.
No one realizes that this is the best meal they'll eat for the next 85 days.
In the distance, a thick black plume of smoke rises into the night,
illuminated by a dull orange glow.
Day 6
Nate stands in line at the pharmacy for 3 hours waiting for Priya's prescription. Inside,
the pharmacist huddles under a headlamp over a cooler of melting ice. He logs every sale by
hand in a notebook. He gives Nate two vials on an IOU and adds Priya's name to the notebook.
20 minutes later, a man charges in, wielding a heavy steel pipe. He walks straight past the line
and demands oxycodone. A local contractor tries to tackle the man, who swings the pipe wildly.
The crack of the contractor’s collarbone fills the pharmacy. The rest of the customers panic
and surge for the exit as the pharmacist dumps an entire shelf worth into a bag and hands it over.
The pharmacy is officially closed.
That afternoon, Nate’s crew is ordered to take the department’s last fueled tanker truck to
the county jail. The facility has a generator, but the deputies have abandoned their posts. The
staff that remains are exhausted. Nobody at the gate will say how many people are locked
inside. During hurricanes, thousands of prisoners were left in flooded cells without food or water.
The tanker drains into a cistern, the gate closes, and nobody signs for the delivery.
Day 7
The hospital runs out of time.
Many hospitals are required to store 96 hours of generator fuel. That deadline passed on
Day 4. A fuel truck arrived yesterday under armed police escort. But it only
delivered half a load. Dana says the entire building is running 1 generator out of 3.
Volunteers are sitting in darkened wards squeezing breathing bags by hand because
the ventilators sit on circuits the last generator can’t reach.
That evening, a man called Hector Ruiz climbs to the roof of Nate’s apartment
building. Hector is a lineman for the electric utility. He’s been home for six hours out
of the last 150. The desperate residents swarm around him as though he’s a prophet.
He tells them he does not know what happened. Neither does anyone he works for.
Whatever hit the grid wiped everything at once. The catastrophic failure focuses on
the large transformers at the substations. These behemoths weigh up to 400 tons and
are built to order. The U.S. imports about 85% of them, mainly from South Korea. Hector tries
to explain how a new one can take 80 to 120 weeks to deliver, but he’s met with groans.
The utilities keep a shared pool of spares,
but that only becomes mandatory after a documented act of terrorism and a
presidential emergency declaration. Nobody has declared anything… yet. Even if they did,
fewer than 20 railcars in the country are capable of moving a machine that heavy.
Since Day 4, the water processing plant has managed to push a pathetic
thin trickle into the west side. It takes 10 excruciating minutes to fill
a bucket from a ground-floor tap. The lobby sink is now the building's only lifeline.
At 9:40p.m.,the operations center radios Nate with a direct order from the director. The treatment
plants are out of diesel. There’s only enough fuel to keep one high-service pump running. Whatever
water remains will go to the hospitals, City Hall, the emergency operations center, and the jail.
Residential service on the west side has been cut. The director issues a kill list of valves.
Valve 114 is on it… Nate's neighborhood.
Nate and one crew member drive out to the valve pit. It’s covered with darkness. The
valve key is a steel bar taller than Nate. It takes 41 turns to close. Midway through,
two shadows emerge from an alley. They throw bottles at Nate and hurl abuse.
The crew member grabs the wrench from Nate and steps forward. The men retreat
back into the shadows, close enough for Nate to feel their eyes on him.
The crew member hands the wrench back and Nate completes the job.
He writes it in the log on the hood of the truck. Day 7, 2215 hours:
Valve 114 closed on the director’s order. West side residential service is suspended.
When he gets home, his panicked neighbors are waiting in the lobby. They hold empty buckets,
desperately asking why the water stopped. One lady screams she saw Nate’s truck near
the valve. He says nothing, he just pushes through the crowd.
Day 9
A ground floor resident opens the basement door and slams it shut again.
The city’s infrastructure is beginning to collapse.
A metropolitan sewer system doesn’t flow downhill all the way to the treatment plant.
It requires mechanical lift stations to pump waste over high points. Their
backup power is only designed for 48 hours. Now, everything the neighborhood flushes,
pours, or buckets down a drain heads for the lowest drain on the block.
And that’s Nate’s basement.
Exactly where Priya’s insulin is located.
At noon, Nate steps into the gloom. He wraps his legs in contractor bags, tapes them tight,
puts on dish gloves and switches on a headlamp. The basement is worse than he imagined. The water
is thigh high. It’s thick, stagnant and the color of weak coffee. Nate wades through the sludge and
finds the Mason jar exactly where he left it. Behind the tires. It’s sealed and dry. The vials
are still cold against his palm. He carries the jar upstairs, holding it in front of him like a
relic. The moment he steps inside his apartment, he throws everything he was wearing away.
Down on the river, people have discovered the storm drain outfalls. A trickle of water seeps
from the pipes and into the Cuyahoga River. A line of residents wait to fill their buckets.
It’s reminiscent of Venezuela's 2019 blackout. Then, the residents of Caracas collected water
at drain pipes along the Guaire River, a channel that also carried the city's sewage.
Day 10
Walt Pruitt collapses in a stairwell and has a violent seizure.
The liquor stores were the second thing looted after the electronics. Walt,
it turns out, had been drinking a quarter bottle a day for years.
When heavy drinkers stop suddenly they can go into alcohol withdrawal. The worst
cases bring seizures, hallucinations, and death.
Dana scours the building and finds a half-full bottle of vodka in a vacant unit. The door has
been kicked in and the apartment turned upside down by residents searching for hoarded food.
Dana flips over a condo board agenda and writes out a dosing schedule. The most
important medication in the building is a shot of Smirnoff every 4 hours,
administered by a registered nurse with a stopwatch.
Day 11
Diarrhea tears through the building like a plague.
Dana sits by a lantern, mixing salt and sugar into boiled water to fight
dehydration. She hands it out in coffee mugs. At 2 in the morning,
Priya starts vomiting. For a diabetic, a stomach bug can be a death sentence. A sick
body burns through insulin at an accelerated rate. Dana sits by Priya’s side until dawn,
checking her blood sugar every hour and dosing from a vial that survived the basement flood.
The meter reads 286. An hour later, 301. Then 254.
Eventually Priya keeps down a cup of the salt water and collapses into sleep.
Day 12
When Nate closed Valve 114, he trapped the remaining water that
was already in the neighborhood's mains. For days,
gravity has been draining that water toward the lowest point in the zone.
Nate knows exactly where that is.
He stands over a dead-end hydrant, 2 blocks from the river,
a heavy wrench in his hands. His hands tremble as he cranks the valve open.
By sunset, 100 people are lined up with pots and buckets. They have no idea
the man who just gave them water was the man who took it away in the first place.
Day 13
Mr. Barry from the fourth floor starts to burn up, his eyes turn red,
his skin goes yellow. He has been drinking from the outfalls for days to save his family's share.
It’s a big mistake.
Rats carry a bacterial infection called leptospirosis in their
urine, and it spreads through contaminated water.
4 men carry Mr. Barry to the hospital on a broken door.
He never comes back.
Day 14
Dana sprints up to the 13th floor. She’s checking on Mrs. Adeyemi,
an 81 year old widow who relies on a plug in oxygen concentrator to survive.
The door is unlocked. Dana pushes it open.
Mrs Adeyemi is still in her armchair, the tubing still in her nose.
She’s been dead for 10 days.
Nobody smelled it. By Day 9, the entire building smelled like death and rotten sewage.
Dana panics. There’s nobody to call. The phones have been dead for 2 weeks.
The only working link to any authority is the radio on Nate's belt. She rushes down stairs.
He calls it into the operations center. 40 minutes later the city
answers. The morgues are full. Lock the door and seal her in.
The news hits the residents like a sledgehammer.
Two men tape plastic sheeting over her door.
Someone spraypaints the date on it and the words, “1 DEAD.”
By the next afternoon, the 13th floor is toxic. The building holds an emergency vote.
Some residents insist she has to go because dead bodies spread disease.
That’s a myth. Bodies from natural disasters do not cause epidemics. The
real disease risk is the basement cesspool everyone has been breathing for a week.
The vote is cast. They’ll bury Mrs. Adeyemi themselves.
4 men carry her stiff and bloated body wrapped in a bedsheet, using flashlights
in the dark. Beam flashes bounce off the wall as they make their descent.
One man slips on a step slick with condensation, almost sending the decaying body of Mrs. Adeyemi
down onto the others. The stairs turn sharply at every floor. The men have
to heave the corpse upright. They can feel the body shift with every jolt and movement.
For 50 minutes, they fight the sliding dead weight, until they reach the lobby.
They bury her in the strip of lawn behind the building. It’s a shallow grave,
only 3 feet (0.9 meters) down. It’s all the 4 exhausted men can dig in the baking
August clay. Priya writes Mrs. Adeyemi's name and date of birth on an index card,
seals it in a Mason jar, and shoves it into the dirt.
Day 16
Hector Ruiz and a crew are sent to bring the hospital back online. They need to hook
up a massive, shipping container sized generator to re-energize the main line.
The power line is supposed to be dead.
It isn’t.
Somewhere on the west side, a desperate homeowner has wired a
portable generator straight into their house. The current is flowing out of
the house and into the utility's lines. It’s called a backfeed and it’s lethal.
Backfeed like this can energize lines that everyone believes are dead,
and it has killed linemen before.
Hector touches the conductor. A blinding blue arc flashes and a
loud bang suddenly fills the alleyway. The high voltage locks Hector’s muscles,
welding his hand to the wire for a second. His lifeless body is thrown to the ground.
His crew don’t bother calling an ambulance. They just bring Hector’s body home in a bucket truck.
The residents dig a second grave behind the building.
That night, Nate stands on the dark roof. In the distance, he can hear the rogue neighborhood
generator humming. He knows it’s out there. He can’t tell which house it is coming from.
Day 17
20 men from across Fulton Road march toward the Valve 114 hydrant with buckets.
Walt has already taped a sign reserving the water for residents of the building.
Nate knows the pipe under the street belongs to everyone, but he says nothing.
One of the outsiders spots Nate’s water department jacket. It’s Dale
Brandt’s brother-in-law. He pushes through the crowd and berates Nate,
accusing him of hoarding water. He grabs Nate by the collar and shoves him to the ground.
Another resident steps in, pushing Dale’s brother-in-law back. Nate gets to his
feet and walks away. The arguing continues for another 4 minutes.
The bloody brawl lasts 1 minute.
Nate watches from the lobby door as the group swing at each other. A building
resident hefts the heavy hydrant cap and lets rip. A jaw breaks with a sickening crunch.
A man drops to the asphalt, his face masked with blood. The outsiders from across Fulton
Road retreat empty handed. The beaten man is Dale’s brother-in-law. Up on the 6th floor,
Dale watches from his balcony. He grips the railing tightly, his knuckles turning white.
Day 18
A rumor erupts across the neighborhood. Perry Nuclear Power Plant, about 40
miles (64 km) away is running out of diesel to cool its pumps.
Nobody bothers to check it.
Panic breaks out.
By noon, thousands of people are fleeing on foot with suitcases, shopping carts,
and children on their shoulders. Interstate 90 is a graveyard of abandoned cars that ran out of gas.
The rumor is never confirmed and never denied.
Half the power plant leaves. Most of them never come back.
That night, Nate steals a master key from Walt's office and slips into the
empty apartments in the building. Every water heater in the building
holds 30 to 50 gallons (114 to 189 liters) of drinkable water.
41 of the units are empty. Nate drains them one by one into buckets and carries
roughly 1,600 gallons (6,057 liters) of life saving water into his apartment.
He doesn’t tell anyone.
Day 20
The heavy brass wrench slips off a stuck hydrant nut. It slices a jagged gash in
Nate’s left forearm from wrist to elbow. Dark red blood seeps from it. Dana washes
the wound with boiled water and closes it with expired butterfly strips from 2021.
Day 22
A man in a reflective vest with a clipboard and a laminated badge arrives in the lobby.
He claims he’s registering residents for federal aid. He asks how many people live in each unit,
what medications they take, and what supplies they have on hand.
Walt eagerly signs the building up first and walks him floor to floor.
Nate awakens to the sound of wood splintering from down the corridor. Peering through the peephole,
he sees 3 masked men battering down the door of an elderly couple in 1104. The
same unit the FEMA official logged as having 6 months supply of canned goods.
The agency had already warned residents about imposters posing as disaster workers. But with
the internet down, nobody in the building saw it.
Screams come from inside the apartment.
Nate throws the door open and rushes down the hall,
just as the 3 men come barrelling out with bags of food. One of them slams into Nate,
sending him crashing to the ground. Nate scrambles to his feet, but all he can see
are torchlight beams across the walls of the stairwell and the sound of heavy boots.
Nate turns back and steps into the ruined apartment. The elderly couple
did what they could. They tried to defend themselves. They’re both dead.
The next morning, 2 new graves are dug behind the apartment building.
Day 24
Dale Brandt corners Nate by the hydrant.
Dale's brother-in-law talked with a former driver for the water department. He knows who turned off
the neighborhood water supply. Now, so does Dale. And in a few hours, the whole building will know.
Dale doesn’t yell. He steps in close, close enough for Nate to feel the heat from his breath.
He tells Nate that he knows Priya walks the same route to the hydrant every morning at
7a.m. He murmurs something about accidents happening in the dark stairwells. Or that
the route to the hydrant is a long way for a young woman who’s all by herself.
Then he tells Nate to open the valve.
Nate sits alone that night thinking it over.
He decides to not open the valve.
Day 26
The city begins digging mass graves in the park.
The families who fled the city left their pets behind. The dogs have formed roaming packs.
The graves are shallow, and the dogs are hungry. Men with shovels have
to stand guard over the corpses to stop them from being dug up.
Day 27
The cut on Nate’s arm is burning hot. Red lines begin to move toward his elbow.
Dana knows that this means.
The pharmacies were looted weeks ago. But the pet store wasn’t. Nobody thought to
raid the fish aisle. Aquarium antibiotics are sold without a prescription and are
unregulated by the FDA. Dana grabs a bottle of fish amoxicillin, calculates the dose for
a 190-pound (86 kg) man, and hands him two yellow capsules with a cup of boiled water.
Day 30
The red lines and heat on Nate’s arms are beginning to fade. The fish amoxicillin worked.
Outside, a National Guard convoy rolled in from the West coast with 3 trucks of
supplies. It’s a drop in the ocean for a city of more than 300,000. The Guardsmen are tired,
underfed, and a very long way from home. It doesn’t take long before a
staff sergeant is trading cases of MREs for jewelry out of the back of a truck.
Priya’s insulin only works if she has food to go with it. The building's pantry is nearly empty.
Dana walks to the drop off point, watching a gaunt sergeant turn away a crying mother.
The very next moment, he hands a crate of MREs to a man who palmed him a gold watch.
Dana slides off her wedding ring,
trading it for a case of 12 meals. She doesn’t mention it at dinner that night.
Walt’s building bylaws are being strictly enforced. Water is rationed by index card.
Doors are locked at dark. Residents take turns guarding the lobby barricade in 2-hour shifts.
The barricade catches Dale's 12-year-old son coming out of the building pantry with a jar
of peanut butter. The board calls an emergency meeting in the lobby by candlelight. A circle
of plastic chairs has been set up, Dale stands in front of the committee. His son
and wife huddle behind, their eyes red. Dale pleads his case. It was a mistake,
the boy was desperate. If his family is thrown out, they’re effectively dead.
No one says a word. Walt clears his throat and starts the vote. One by one,
the residents vote. Dale locks eyes with Nate. He knows about the valve.
Nate swallows hard and thinks about Priya. He raises his hand in favor.
Day 33
Just after midnight, Dale Brandt sneaks back for the rest of his
family’s things. The man on barricade duty is a retired mail carrier with a
.308 caliber hunting rifle. He sees a shape climbing the fence behind the loading dock.
He doesn’t shout a warning.
He just fires.
Nate writes it in the log later that morning. Day 33, 0120 hours:
D. Brandt shot at rear barricade. Deceased.
He puts the pen down and stares at his hands, as though he personally signed Dale’s death warrant.
Day 35
It’s been a month without electricity.
Priya finds a shortwave radio in an abandoned apartment. She runs to the
roof and cranks it to life. What she hears sounds almost surreal.
Montreal is reading the weather and the hockey scores. Quebec runs its own grid,
and it never went down. Houston is advertising a patio furniture sale. Walt listens for a full
minute and mutters it’s the first time in history anyone has envied Texas for its power grid.
Day 38
The temperature drops to 34 degrees F (1 C). Desperate for warmth,
a family of 4 brings their charcoal grill inside and closes the windows.
They never wake up.
They’re found in the morning, dead from carbon monoxide poisoning.
Four more holes are dug in the lawn out back. The graveyard is growing.
That afternoon, Nate carries everything they own down 8 flights to an empty
unit on the third floor. It is warmer and closer to the water.
But it’s also easier to break into.
Day 41
300 frustrated people line up at the hydrant with paint buckets, trash cans,
and a fish tank. Nate holds the wrench. Two steps behind him is the retired mail carrier,
brandishing the deer rifle that killed Dale Brandt.
Nobody argues or skips the line.
Day 47
Nate builds a makeshift stove from a paint can and a length of dryer vent.
They burn the dining chairs first, then the bookshelf, and then a three-ring binder from
Nate's office titled August 2003 Blackout: Lessons Learned. It burns for 11 minutes.
The West Side Market has transformed into a lawless barter hall. A D-cell
battery buys a dozen eggs. A carton of cigarettes buys almost anything.
Dusk arrives a little earlier now and is the real curfew. After dark,
the streets belong to whoever has a flashlight and a weapon.
On the shortwave radio, news arrives secondhand and out of order. There are fires in Pittsburgh.
Relief camps have opened outside Columbus. Canadian aid convoys are stuck out at the
Detroit border waiting for paperwork from a government nobody can seem to reach.
Day 52
Nate discovers a column of tally marks on the inside back cover of Priya’s school notebook.
He feels a wave of panic sweep over him. She’s been skipping
her evening dose every other day for weeks. She did the math on the
remaining vials and decided the family couldn’t afford to keep her alive..
Day 55
The first hard freeze hits the city.
The water inside in a dead main freezes, expands, shattering the cast iron pipes. By morning the
dead-end hydrant produces nothing but a brown crust of ice. The city’s system is destroyed. The
majority of the water department crew run, trying to find food and sanctuary for their families.
That evening, Dana leans over Priya's bed. Her breath smells sweet, like nail polish
remover. Priya is panting heavily. It’s diabetic ketoacidosis. Without insulin,
it can kill a Type 1 diabetic within days. Dana injects her with the last
full vial and stays awake all night, watching her daughter.
Day 57
The gas pressure suddenly comes back for six hours. Nobody knows why.
A man on West 50th Street opens the valve on his furnace, strikes a match. The
explosion levels the entire house. When the firefighters dig through the rubble,
they find a portable generator in the basement wired straight into the house panel.
The low humming sound Nate has heard from the roof every night
has stopped. It was the same makeshift generator that had electrocuted Hector.
Nate smiles before catching himself. Justice for Hector.
Day 58
The shortwave crackles with the first federal statement in 8 weeks. A Department of Energy
official is speaking from an undisclosed location. He praises the resilience of the
American people and announces that power will be restored in phases over the next 12 to 18 months.
He does not say what happened, or which phase Cleveland is in.
Day 60
The hospital needs an ICU nurse more than it needs anything else,
and it pays in insulin. Dana makes the difficult decision to move into the
green zone that afternoon with a duffel bag and a promise to send vials home by
courier twice a week. A resident will stay with Priya while Nate is at work.
That evening, the plant supervisor hands Nate the current valve map for the west
side. Every residential valve on the west side is marked closed, as ordered.
But Nate spots an anomaly. One transmission main is marked open that was not on the
director's list. It runs east along the lakefront to an affluent suburb. Beside it,
a handwritten note says, "Diesel, 4,000 gallons (15,142 liters) weekly."
Nate stares at the map. He feels a weight on his chest. Everything clicks into place.
The plant's last working pump runs on diesel. The wealthy suburb has
been draining fuel from the nearby marina's tanks and the boats tied
up in its slips. They aren’t sharing power, they’re bartering water for fuel.
The supply Nate shut off on day 7, that act turned his basement into a cesspool and
forced his neighbors into drinking toxic water, is the currency that’s bought the
diesel. The diesel that kept the plant online. That kept the hospital running.
Day 71
Walt Pruitt sits in his recliner in his apartment on the 9th floor.
His eyes are wide, staring blankly at the wall.
Nate crouches down in front of him. He gently closes Walt’s eyes.
When the residents clear out his unit, they uncover a sick betrayal. In a desk drawer,
they find the carbon copies from the fake FEMA man’s clipboard. Walt wasn’t fooled like the
rest of them. He was in on it. Empty vodka bottles are littered across the apartment. Walt had traded
the list of the best-stocked apartments in the building for liquor… and the elderly couple died.
The guilt was too much.
The residents hold a vote to bury Walt’s body. It doesn’t pass. Nate and one other
resident do it anyway. Walt’s body is laid to rest next to the same couple he sold out.
Day 77
Priya’s body gives out. The weeks of severe rationing have caught up with
her. Her breathing slows. Nate shakes her by the shoulders, but she doesn’t move.
Nate screams her name.
Nothing.
She has slipped into a coma.
Day 78
The courier from the hospital never arrives.
Nate searches the snow covered streets and finds him face down in the drift. He was just
2 blocks from the hospital. His pockets have been turned out and the insulin cooler gone.
On the west side, a vial of insulin is worth more than a gun.
Nate treks to the green zone gate with his plant badge. The guards turn him away.
Dana rushes to the fence 20 minutes later and passes three smuggled vials through the mesh.
They manage to lock fingers for a brief moment, then Nate makes the journey back to his daughter.
It’ll be the last time he sees his wife… and they were separated by a security fence.
That night, Nate kneels by his daughter’s side and loads a syringe by candlelight.
His hand shakes as he punctures Priya’s skin and presses the plunger. Within hours,
her breath stabilizes. Her eyelids begin to flutter.
Nate collapses beside her bed.
Day 80
The building’s defence collapses.
The retired mail carrier is found at the lobby barricade with his throat slashed.
His deer rifle is missing. Everyone knows the people on Fulton Road did it.
And now, they have a hunting rifle.
Day 83
The marina drains its last boat of diesel fuel. There’s nothing left to trade. The mains are dry.
The city is about to flatline.
Day 86
The neighborhood across the street has reached its limit. It begins tearing itself apart.
Nate stands on his building roof and watches as two men come to blows over a crate of MREs.
A punch is thrown. Moments later, a retaliatory firebomb ignites the wooden framed structure. The
blaze completely guts the structure, lighting up the night until it's nothing but a charred,
smoking ruin. One of the casualties trapped inside is the brother-in-law of Dale Brandt.
Nate turns away and heads back down to his daughter.
Day 90
It’s Thanksgiving. Nate and Priya eat cold MREs next to Dana’s empty chair.
On the shortwave, the President speaks from a hidden bunker,
repeating the same hollow praise for American resilience.
At 6 p.m., a loud pounding rattles the lobby doors. Nate and a few residents join the guard,
preparing for the worst. The iron wrench hangs by Nate’s side.
Standing in the freezing twilight is a woman. Next to her, a 12-year-old boy wearing an
oversized coat. It is Dale Brandt's widow and the boy Nate voted to expel into the streets.
She looks Nate in the eyes and asks for shelter and food.
Nate grips the wrench and looks at the boy wearing his dead father’s coat,
then the charred shell of the building opposite. He glances at the other residents
who shake their heads. Nate tells her that he can’t help. He repeats the empty lie he
has been telling everyone, muttering everything will be fine in the end.
The widow and the boy turn away, their feet crunching on the snow.
Nate watches them for a moment, then turns away.
That night, Nate steps out into the street. For the first time that he can remember it’s quiet.
There’s no alarms, no screaming or shouting. It’s almost eerie.
Suddenly, a deafening crack splits the air.
A high velocity .308 tears cleanly through his left shoulder. The force
spins him around and sends him crashing to the ground. Dark blood spills out,
staining the snow. Nate’s breath hangs in the air as he cranes his neck, looking for the shooter.
Across the street, he sees a shadow. Small, slight… wearing an oversized coat. In his hands,
he’s holding the mailman’s hunting rifle, the barrel still smoking.
The boy doesn’t run. He just cycles the bolt, a brass casing dropping softly
into the snow. He raises the rifle and aims the scope at Nate’s chest…

is hit by the fallout of a nearby nuclear explosion? Watch “World War
